'''Coto Makassar''' or Coto Mangkasara ([[Makassarese language|Makassarese]]), is an Indonesian traditional soup originating from [[Makassar]], [[South Sulawesi]]. It is a variant of ''[[Soto (food)|soto]],'' traditionally made with [[beef]], [[offal]] [[stew]] with seasoned broth made from ground [[peanut]]s and [[spices]].<ref>{{cite book | title = Lonely Planet Indonesia | author1 = Loren Bell | author2 = Stuart Butler| author3 = Trent Holden | author4 =Anna Kaminski| author5 =Hugh McNaughtan| author6 =Adam Skolnick| author7 =Iain Stewart| author8 =Ryan Ver Berkmoes | publisher=Lonely Planet| year=2016 | isbn=9781760341619 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=6HCGDAAAQBAJ&q=Coto+Makassar+beef&pg=PT1632}}</ref> The main ingredient of this soup is [[beef]], and it can be mixed with innards, such as intestine, liver, lungs, heart, tripe, or [[cow]] brain. The spices are used both for flavouring, and to balance the richness of the meat.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Pradiati |first=Savira Rizki |date=2023-11-17 |title=Historical Gastronomy of Coto Makassar |url=https://ejournal.upi.edu/index.php/gastur/article/view/63523 |journal=The Journal Gastronomy Tourism |volume=10 |issue=2 |pages=203–210 |doi=10.17509/gastur.v10i2.63523 |issn=2716-3970|doi-access=free }}</ref>

The soup originates in the 16th-century in the [[Sultanate of Gowa]], and was originally cooked for royal servants and soldiers<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Prastowo |first1=Indro |last2=Nurusman |first2=Arief Abdillah |last3=Moro |first3=Hendro Kusumo Eko Prasetyo |last4=Rizkianti |last5=Dewi |first5=Cyntia |date=2023-06-01 |title=Diversity of Indonesian offal-based dishes |journal=Journal of Ethnic Foods |language=en |volume=10 |issue=1 |pages=15 |doi=10.1186/s42779-023-00181-8 |doi-access=free |issn=2352-6181}}</ref>. While it is now eaten regularly as a breakfast food in the region, it retains an association with weddings and religious celebrations.<ref name=":0" />

Coto Makassar is usually served with [[Burasa]] or [[Ketupat]] rice cakes and [[Tauco]] sauce, a savoury fermented soybean paste. The use of Tauco indicates that the dish is influenced by [[Chinese Indonesian cuisine]]<ref name=":0" />, and the use of Indian curry spices, imported peanuts and halal meat point to the cultural diversity of Makassar during the Gowa period.<ref name=":1" />
